title: Smart Speakers With No Screen: Echo Dot, Google Home Speaker and HomePod mini 2 for Reminders and Timers
subtitle: A plain-English look at three small speakers you talk to, what they can help with around the house, and what they can quietly cost after the free trials end.
excerpt: A small speaker that answers to your voice can set a kitchen timer, tell you the weather and play an audiobook with no screen to fuss over. Here is how the Echo Dot, Google Home Speaker and HomePod mini 2 compare, including the fees and the limits.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: The pasta is boiling, your hands are wet, and you cannot remember whether you set the oven timer. Or you want the weather before your walk but your reading glasses are in the other room. Small jobs like these are where a voice-only smart speaker earns its spot on the counter.

These speakers have no screen. You speak, and they answer out loud. That makes them simple to live with, but it also means they are not right for everyone. If you would rather read a reminder or see a grandchild on a video call, a smart display with a screen is the better fit, and we cover those in a separate guide. People with severe hearing loss who need to see text may also be poorly served by a speaker that only talks. An audiologist can talk through options.

All three speakers listen for a wake word, a short phrase that tells the speaker you are talking to it, and then carry out what you ask. The Echo Dot and Google Home Speaker pages mention connecting to Wi-Fi, and the Google speaker is set up with the Google Home app. The Echo Dot comes with a Quick Start Guide, and the HomePod mini 2 comes with documentation.

The three speakers come from Amazon, Google and Apple. The Echo Dot works with Amazon Alexa, the Google speaker uses Gemini, and the HomePod mini 2 uses Siri only, according to Reviewed. The Apple HomePod mini 2 needs an Apple device, so it is not a fit for someone with an Android phone. We have not confirmed which phones the other two work with, so check the maker's page before buying.

One honest caution about reminders: a small 2020 University of Maryland study followed seven older adults who rarely used technology. The researchers reported that most participants "did not find the reminders or alarms reliable," and some worried that a power or internet outage would stop them. A speaker is handy for everyday nudges, but it should not be the only thing standing between someone and an important dose of medicine.

items: Ongoing fees: check what happens when a free trial ends. The Google speaker's Premium features stop after its trial, and Apple Music switches to a monthly charge. Apple also says some AI features will be available for a fee in the future.
Which phone you have: the HomePod mini 2 needs an Apple device. Check the maker's page for the other two before you buy.

A mic mute control you can find: Consumer Reports says smart speakers have a switch to turn off the microphone. The Google speaker has one on the bottom, and the Echo Dot has a mic-off button. We do not have details on where Apple's is.
Simple physical controls: the Echo Dot lets you tap the top to snooze an alarm, which is easy when you are half awake.
Sound quality for the room: PCWorld says cheaper speakers give decent sound in small rooms only, and that the HomePod mini has the best audio in its size class.
Shipping: if buying from a senior-focused seller such as Lively, check delivery times and costs before you order.
Hearing and screens: a voice-only speaker gives no visual text, so it may not suit someone with severe hearing loss.
Setup help: plan for a family member to help on day one if setting up an app or account is unfamiliar.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Put the speaker where you spend the most time, often the kitchen, and plug it in. For the Google speaker, you then use the Google Home app on a phone to join Wi-Fi and a Google account. For the others, follow the guide in the box. As a general tip, set it up together with a relative so the account details are written down somewhere safe.

Start with two or three things you will use every day: a cooking timer, the morning weather and perhaps an audiobook. Once those feel natural, add a reminder or two, and test that each one actually goes off. Try a few spoken phrasings until you find the ones the speaker understands best.

If you are uneasy about a speaker that listens, consider using the mute control at night or during private conversations. With the Google speaker muted, it will not respond to your voice but can still play audio.

A smart speaker is not a medical alert device. It will not call for help after a fall unless it is paired with a separate, paid service. Some models can notify family if an older person does not interact with the speaker by a set time each day, according to Consumer Reports. The Google and Apple speakers can listen for the sound of a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, but on the Google speaker that sound detection is listed under the Standard plan, which costs $10 a month after the 30-day trial. Apple's own page says its feature "should not be relied upon in circumstances where you may be harmed." Keep working smoke and CO alarms, and in an emergency, call 911. For medication schedules, ask your doctor or pharmacist about the safest way to stay on track.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: For many households, a small speaker that sets timers and answers simple questions is a pleasant, low-fuss helper. Pick the one that matches the phones in your family, keep an eye on the fees after the trials, and treat it as a friendly assistant rather than a safety net.

products.name: Echo Dot (5th Gen)
products.price: $79.99 (regular price at Lively, November 2026); check current price, as it may be lower elsewhere
products.blurb: Reviewed, relaying Wirecutter's picks, names the Echo Dot for beginners. It offers hands-free timers and weather, a tap-the-top snooze and a mic-off button. The Lively page states no subscription, and shipping is $8 for economy (free over $25).

products.name: Google Home Speaker
products.price: $79.99, down from $99.99 (Google Store, November 2026); check current price
products.blurb: Suits people who want to set reminders and calendar invites by speaking, with a light ring that shows when it is listening. It includes a 30-day trial of Google Home Premium Standard; afterward Premium features stop, only a more basic Gemini for Home remains, and Standard costs $10 a month or $100 a year (Advanced is $20 a month or $200 a year).

products.name: HomePod mini 2
products.blurb: Suits iPhone and iPad users who care about sound; PCWorld says the HomePod mini has the best audio in its size class. Siri is its only assistant, and the Siri AI is "coming in a future software update" and needs an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad. Apple says some AI features "will be available for a fee in the future," and Apple Music costs $11.99 a month after a 3-month trial.
